highlights: Japan held its first post-war general election on 10 April with 72.1% turnout, electing thirty-nine women to the Diet under newly granted suffrage.
Premier Kijuro Shidehara and his Cabinet resigned en bloc on 22 April amid inter-party pressure following the general election.
An indictment containing 55 counts against 28 major Japanese war criminals was filed with the International Military Tribunal for the Far East on 29 April.
The United States Education Mission submitted its report recommending administrative decentralization, curriculum democratization, language simplification, and tuition-free coeducational schooling.
General Orders No. 18 established the Diplomatic Section as a Special Staff Section under SCAP on 18 April 1946.
An Imperial Ordinance establishing the Holding Company Liquidation Commission was approved by SCAP and promulgated by the Japanese Government on 20 April.
The first restitution of identifiable looted property occurred on 12 April when two Hong Kong fire engines were returned to British authorities.

summary: This seventh monthly report covers non-military activities of the Allied occupation in Japan during April 1946, a pivotal month marked by the nation's first post-war general election on 10 April. The election witnessed widespread popular participation, the debut of female suffrage with thirty-nine women elected to the Diet, and a moderate conservative victory that precipitated the en bloc resignation of the Shidehara Cabinet on 22 April. The report documents major political and legal milestones, notably the publication of the simplified draft constitution, the expansion and amendment of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East charter, and the filing of formal indictments against twenty-eight major war criminals. Economically, SCAP monitored persistent urban food deficits, post-conversion currency circulation, the establishment of the Economic Stabilization Board, and the dissolution of wartime control companies alongside rapid trade union growth. In social affairs, the report highlights the United States Education Mission recommendations, public health campaigns containing typhus and cholera, and the repatriation of over two million Japanese nationals. For historians, this summation provides invaluable statistical data, government directives, and institutional records detailing Japan’s early post-war democratization and economic restructuring.
